state.misconception_label: Believes if you changed all values by the same proportion the range would not change

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: Tom and Katie are discussing the \( 5 \) plants with these heights: \( 24 \mathrm{~cm}, 17 \mathrm{~cm}, 42 \mathrm{~cm}, 26 \mathrm{~cm}, 13 \mathrm{~cm} \) Tom says if all the plants were cut in half, the range wouldn't change. Katie says if all the plants grew by \( 3 \mathrm{~cm} \) each, the range wouldn't change. Who do you agree with? I got Only
Tom because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Can you explain why you think the range wouldn't change if all the plants were cut in half or grew by 3 cm each? What about the concept of range leads you to believe that?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I thought that if you cut all the plants in half, the biggest and smallest would still be the same distance apart, so the range wouldn't change. And for Katie, I thought adding the same amount to each height wouldn't change the difference between the tallest and shortest either. But now I'm not sure if that’s really right. Can you help me understand how the range actually works?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Can you think of any examples where changing all values by the same proportion would actually change the range?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher's final question contains a critical mathematical error (asking about proportional change when the student correctly reasoned about it in Turn 2), fails to acknowledge that the student actually had the right reasoning for Katie's case, and provides no evidence that the student's understanding improved since they never get to respond to the flawed prompt.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses probing questions to guide the student's thinking (asking about their reasoning in Turn 1, prompting them to consider counterexamples in Turn 3) and never directly provides the answer, which is textbook Socratic method.
